utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue. And I encourage you to be as brief as possible, and bear in mind that you don't have to ask questions on every issue raised in cross-examination. Just confine yourself to those matters where you think your witness might need some rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Kostic, in connection with the assertions made by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff with respect to my open letter to Milan Babic which she refers to as my statement - she can call it whatever she likes - but do you have the letter in front of you? It's Exhibit 352, tab 79, and it is the front page of the Politika newspaper.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you read out what it says from the beginning, that first part, and then we can go on to some others.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Open letter of Slobodan Milosevic to Milan Babic. The people should not have to suffer because of the self-love of a politician. To reject -- the rejection of the continued peaceful course of the solution to the crisis means to opt for a continuation of war at a time when there are no more reasons for war. The fact that Serbia is giving comprehensive and selfless assistance to Krajina does not mean that you have gained the right to decide upon the lives of its citizens."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're reading that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subtitles, subheadings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine, the subheadings. Let's not waste time with that. Let's go to the original text of the -- the actual text of the letter, although that is part of the text, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I feel it my obligation and responsibility to express my disagreement with your position that you do not want the United Nations peacekeeping forces to protect the territory of Krajina under the Cyrus Vance Plan. Rejecting protection --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, to what end is this letter being read, and how much of it is going to be read? Why don't you just put your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask a question, and it relates to the claim made that I am bringing into question the Krajina leadership and everything over there presented by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff referring to the book by Borisav Jovic, and that from this letter you can see that it's absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read the penultimate paragraph of the letter, if you will.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Since it has become obvious that for a long time now you are creating an image with the citizens of Krajina, that you are agreeing with the leadership of Serbia on your positions and stands, I'd like the people of Krajina to know that that is not true."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Professor Kostic, was that the practice? Was that what was done, that over there, and here too for that matter, we can encounter things like that, that what is being done over there is being decided upon in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's what I said in the cross-examination as well. And where my speech was shown and my address to the citizens of Glina, that we had come there to tell the people that the rumours going round there were just not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the constant practice, that is to say that everything that was happening over there was being ascribed to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And during the examination-in-chief, I already said that it was quite wrong to believe, regardless of the fact that you had the greatest political authority and wielded the greatest political influence on the territory of Serbia and the territory of Montenegro, that it was quite wrong to assume, as the public, both national an international, thought, that you had absolute control and influence over the leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, what does it say further on there? "Although you personally informed me that the Presidency decision with respect to the arrival of the UN forces you would accept as a whole, on the whole --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not hearing anything. I just hear the interpretation now in French. I'm receiving the French interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the channels have been mixed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's try again, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the last paragraph, what it says there. "Although you personally informed me --" have you found that? "-- that you would accept entirely the decision of the Yugoslavia Presidency --" that is the SFRY Presidency --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Although you personally informed me that you would accept entirely the decision of the Yugoslavia Presidency on the arrival of the United Nations forces, you have turned a deaf ear to the explicit positions of the Yugoslav Presidency of the Serbian leadership more than once, giving yourself the right to make decisions for which, unfortunately, the entire Serbian people should pay, and pay with their blood."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said about this relationship as contained in my statement, as she called it, and found in Jovic's book, that Krajina not be given any more assistance and support, what does it say at the end of that letter of mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Serbia will not stop helping the people of Krajina even when peace is established, but the citizens of Krajina should know that because of what you have done, you have lost all the trust we had in you, and for future relations with the authorities of the Republic of Serbia, they have to delegate persons who will hold the interests of their people above personal political prestige ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who, then, in my letter has lost trust, or forfeited trust? Is it the people in Krajina, is it the leadership in Krajina, or is it Milan Babic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is any replacement called for here except for saying we don't want to do anything more with him who is -- because he is a liar and a dishonourable man?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And he even publicly accused us of wanting to arrest him and that he was afraid and that he was afraid to spend time in Belgrade, whereas in fact he spent a lot of time in Belgrade frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. He's not the only man that said that. Mesic said he was afraid too, and so did Ante Markovic. He said he was afraid too, so he's not the only one, and nothing happened to any of them. Nobody even whistled at them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Booed them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- You are to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, in this regard and the fact that Babic was replaced after that, my question to you is who replaced Babic? Did we replace him or was he replaced by the Krajina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Assembly of the Republic of Srpska Krajina that replaced him. The initiative came, proposals came from the Assembly session that I attended where the Assembly ultimately adopted the Vance Plan and there were proposals put forward that Mr. Babic be replaced. However, those of us who came to expound the Vance Plan and to convince the delegates of Serbian Krajina that it was a good idea to accept the plan, we suggested that they should not go forward with this at that session, especially as Mr. Babic did not attend the meeting. They did that at a later session, when they were alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the claim that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff made with reference to Borisav Jovic's book, she read out something to the effect that I managed the negotiations on the Vance Plan. Now, do you happen to remember whether Vance and his associates talked to the leadership of Montenegro, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did talk to the leadership of Montenegro at a villa in Gorica in Podgorica and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they talked about Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They talked with me. They talked with the leadership of Krajina, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They talked to you too?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they talked to Tudjman. So was it quite obvious from all that what they actually wanted to achieve? Did they want to talk to all the important factors in Yugoslavia or just to me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they wished to talk to everybody who could have an influence on a positive relationship and the implementation of Cyrus Vance's peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, from those competent individuals, did they leave anybody out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. They talked to us in the Presidency most because they had an interest in seeing that, as the Supreme Command, we should act in conformity with the plan, which means that the Yugoslav People's Army should be withdrawn from that territory once the Blue Helmets arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they talked to you most and then they talked to the leadership of Serbia, Croatia, Montenegro, and Krajina.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Even Mr. Marek Goulding I think went to Krajina on two occasions to explain the plan and to dissuade -- and to prevail upon the leadership in Serb Krajina about some doubts that they had, to prevail upon them to change their minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in connection to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's question to the effect that the Serb Assembly decided who would represent Kosovo and Vojvodina, did the Serbian Assembly make any decisions at all with respect to representation in the Presidency from Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember under what circumstances the Serbian Assembly took over the authorisation and competencies of the Assembly of Kosovo, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I'm not sure I can give the right answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I'm not going to lead you in an answer to the question and suggest one. Madam Uertz-Retzlaff presented an excerpt from Momir Bulatovic, from page 93, dating back to the times we discussed the new constitution of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And she quoted passage, or, rather, the end of a passage, the second passage on page 93, where it says: "Slobodan Milosevic, as usual, had the main say," and here it says: "Slobodan Milosevic, as usually, had the main say on behalf of the other -- in front of the other side." Now, which other side discussed -- or which other sides discussed the Yugoslav constitution? Which were they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't interpret what it says in Momir's book, but I can confirm that several of us most responsible people from Serbia and Montenegro, including Jovic as member of the Presidency from Serbia and myself as member of the Montenegrin Presidency, did take part in those talks. They were held in Belgrade once and once in Vila Gorica, until we finally reached an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, those two sides, Serbia and Montenegro, are those the sides referred to here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here he says: "Slobodan Milosevic took the floor and chaired --" was that Serbia on behalf of the other side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it should be Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who else would be best placed to conduct negotiations in the name of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the constitution, it was you and according -- and it was him for Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was president of the Presidency of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There's an explanation here about how we talked in your villa at Dedinje, or I don't know whose villa at Dedinje. I didn't note it down and it was a few days ago. And that we went out to talk in the garden because there was a waiter there. Do you remember that, what Madam Uertz-Retzlaff explained here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I remember reading about it in Jovic's book. I didn't have time then to say that never did you and Mr. Jovic come to my home except on one occasion when you arrived with a man from the building management a month before I retired from Belgrade, and you asked if I would mind moving to another villa, also on Dedinje, because there had to be some alterations made to the villa, and of course I agreed because I had an apartment in that villa, just as Mesic, Drnovsek, Tupurkovski and others did. But they had already left, so the villa was vacant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we never visited you in your home?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about what it says here, that we had to go out to talk in the garden because there was a waiter in the villa serving coffee?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say it sounds very convincing, just as he said very convincingly that we had coffee together at Batajnica, although I was never there with him on that day. He probably visited that villa very often, so it wasn't difficult for him to describe the atmosphere of the villa. I don't know who he was trying to damage, you or me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you stated quite clearly here that you retired from political life in June when your term of office expired and when the president of the SRJ was elected; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Six months later, in December 1992, you agreed to be a candidate for president of Montenegro. Why in December 1992 did you agree to this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still in Belgrade holding office there, and also after I retired from political life, the relations between the leaderships of Serbia and Montenegro grew increasingly tense. I wasn't afraid that Serbia would attack Montenegro but I was afraid of internal conflicts in Montenegro. As I had decided to retire from political life -- for two years I had been president of Montenegro, before that I had been vice-president of Montenegro, I had also been vice-president of Yugoslavia -- so I felt it was my moral duty to warn the citizens of Montenegro that the then leadership, which is still in power today, were leading them towards separatism, but they were doing it secretly, undercover, because they knew if they did it openly they would not have the support of the people. The only way to be reported in the media was to become a candidate for president. I was nominated by two local communes, my native local commune, and I agreed. Even before the results were announced, I stated I did not expect to win the election but I felt I had done my civic duty of warning the population what was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This reply's quite sufficient. Just another brief clarification in connection with this statement. Was it I who nominated you? You just said that two local communes from your native region nominated you. Did I play any role in your nomination for the candidacy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for a single instant. We never even spoke on the phone. Mr. Jovic called me on the phone once, and he said, "Branko, withdraw. You don't stand a chance of winning." And I told him the same thing that I have now stated before this Court, that I wasn't interested in holding the office but that I wanted to have the chance of telling the citizens of Montenegro where their leadership was taking them. It's well known that practically everything we agreed about the constitution, about common functions at the top, that they instead of unified, transformed this into joint. So there was a Joint Command, every republic had its own embassies, and so on and so forth, and Mr. Bulatovic even agreed that they should switch every six months. It was a hybrid construct that had no chance of surviving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff dwelt for a relatively long time on your conversation with the minister of the interior. That's in tab 1. Would you please take a look at it. She quoted some portions of this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at page 14, where you say at the bottom of the page, last paragraph: "However, the most important problem now --" what does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just find page 14. I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, allow the Trial Chamber to find it. You should be directing us to the page in English. What page is it in the English text, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I don't have the English in my -- oh, yes, I have. Yes I have. Just a moment. I'll find it for you. It's on page 8, the second paragraph not counting the one that's gone over from the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "However, we now have a more serious problem, Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the constitution of Yugoslavia and the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we have three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Muslims are the most numerous and make up about 44 to 46 per cent of the populations. The Serbs make up 32 per cent and have about 64 per cent of the territory. The Croats make up 18 per cent of the population. "According to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina currently in force, all three peoples have equal rights, regardless of their numbers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then questions are put to you, "Who are the Muslims?" And then you say, "... in 95 or 98 per cent of the cases, they are Islamised Serbs, Serbs who accepted Islam, that is."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff quoted to you the next portion, three paragraphs down, where you say: "In 105 of 110 municipalities they live together mixed together."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this one of the key arguments supporting what you say, that the three peoples should agree among themselves?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. In this kind of mixed population, mixed according to ethnic and religious affiliation, it was impossible to draw some kind of demarcation line. That's why we kept saying and insisting that Bosnia should remain entire and whole and unified and as such be part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the next page, and this was also partly quoted by

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "Unfortunately the European Community and Mr. Badinter as president of the Arbitration Commission suggested that a referendum be carried out among the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This means applying the principle of predominance and destroying the principle of equal rights of all three peoples in line with the constitution," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would lead directly to military conflict in Bosnia. Therefore, the idea of internationally recognising an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina leads directly to a conflagration of war of unprecedented dimensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is this what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what Carrington, Cyrus Vance, and others said about these premature recognitions and their influence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than once both Mr. Carrington and Mr. Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen reiterated that the premature recognition of the independence of Slovenia and Croatia, and especially of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had led to escalating war conflicts and fanned the flames, and that it was a disaster for all the peoples on the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please find page 18.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The third paragraph from the bottom, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For us every solution is acceptable resulting from an agreement between each of the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Any attempt by two of the peoples to impose their will on the third will obviously lead to conflict." I think this is fully in line with the provisions of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina which I presented to Their Honours after the end of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said that you were mentioning ideas which would lead to the division of Bosnia, I won't go back to your responses, but look at the second paragraph of your speech here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "But in the event of cantonisation, the Serbs and Muslims could probably work out how to create a division as far as Sarajevo is concerned, because the starting point for cantonisation is the principle of an ethnic majority within a given area. Cantonisation would mean a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would allow the Croats and Serbs to have communications and links with their home states, Croatia and Serbia; in other words, Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the Cutileiro Plan a plan that proposed cantonisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. The Cutileiro Plan was based on precisely those principles, as was the case with the Dayton Accord which led to the end of the war in Bosnia, and it included even some specific links between the Serbian Republic and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We think there is an extremist Muslim fundamentalism about in this wing of the Muslim party. Independence for Bosnia and Herzegovina is an attempt to form the first Islamic state in Europe. We believe that if the Muslim leaders really were to protect the interests of their people, they themselves would have to support the preservation and interests of Yugoslavia, because after the Serbs, the Muslims are the people who are most widely scattered around Yugoslavia. And just as the Serbs naturally want to stay living in a single state, it is also natural for the Muslims to want to live in a single state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You needn't go on. You needn't explain where the Muslims live and so on. You go on to say that the current leaders are not taking into account the interests of the Muslim people. Does this correspond to what their leader Adil Zulfikarpasic was saying, both in the interview we tendered here and in his public interviews?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying here to the minister of foreign affairs of friendly nation Zimbabwe in faraway Africa - and this was all happening in 1992 - and what Mr. Zulfikarpasic wrote about and gave an extensive interview about in 1996 or 1997, these two things, what I said then and the assessments of Mr. Zulfikarpasic, correspond fully. It's not because they correspond but because it's really common sense. That's why I said that Mr. Zulfikarpasic was one of the most eminent intellectuals from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what you say in the third paragraph from the bottom here: "When the Yugoslav crisis began, we had people from Croatia in six of the most responsible positions." What does it go on to say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Six of the most responsible positions in the federation: Mr. Mesic as president of the Presidency, Mr. Markovic as president of the Federal Executive Council, SIV, Mr. Loncar as minister of foreign affairs," and so on. In my examination-in-chief, I also mentioned Mr. Zekan, the minister of finance, and -- his name escapes me now. He was the minister of technology and science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Marendic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bozidar Marendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were many questions about the election of Mesic. Did anyone ever challenge the right of Croatia to elect Mesic as a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one ever denied it for a moment, nor did anyone deny the right of Croatia to provide its own candidate for president in that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the Rules of Procedure where it speaks about the Presidency, does it say that he has to be elected or does he automatically take up the post according to the rotation system?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he had to be elected. He was always elected. But as I explained previously, every member of the Presidency had gone through the various checks in the socialist system, but Mr. Mesic had not gone through this procedure because in the meantime the League of Socialists had been disbanded or, rather, the Socialist Alliance of Working People.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff played several videos concerning your visit to Borovo Selo. I'm not going to play them again because I don't want to waste time, but has it been said more than once, and I have in front of me the English version of the transcript of what you said, you say: "[In English] In this and in all other cases the Federal Executive Council must be fully responsible for it regardless of ethnic affiliation of population overtaken by misfortune."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just finish the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Last sentence: "[In English] Our army must be the power and the national army in the proper sense of the word that will protect -- that will protect and every of our citizens at risk, regardless of his nationality or religion or his political commitment." [Interpretation] That is what you said then in that area, speaking among Serbs, talking about the fact that the army and the leadership would be protecting everybody. Who was attacked there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian population. They were the most numerous among the 8.000 refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So to them, the people who had been attacked and whom you had come to visit after all that, you were saying, "We will be protecting everybody regardless of ethnicity." Was that the crux of your message?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the essence of my message. And it was played several times, and I'm glad it was played. I wouldn't change a single word even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that also express the position of the then leadership concerning equality among ethnicities and non-discrimination?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That reflected the position of all of us who were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia and equality among all the peoples and nations and republics that constituted the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at the time of the visit, of your visit, how many refugees had already come from those parts into Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. About 8.000. Of course there were some Croats among them who had fled to Serbia as well. But since those areas were mostly populated by Serbs, the most refugees were Serbs, and the majority of them were in fact women and children because the men had stayed behind to try to defend their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff has tried to represent that you were attacked by your own colleagues, university professors. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those attacks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All those attacks that were made against you at that time, verbal attacks, did you publish them all in your book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I quoted them verbatim. There were three successive writings, and in all of them they reiterated that they were not criticising me as a person but my political activities and engagement. But the bottom line is that all those people who wrote that did not make up even 10 per cent of the staff of the university. Of course all those who signed those statements had been and remain in opposition parties, people who were always my opponents, because even today we have different opinions as far as politics are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just looking for another passage. Some of the questions asked by the opposite side had to do with rallies, and you said something about them being organised from behind the scenes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff told you that you had spoken then about events that were totally made up because the wave of refugees and the violence started later, whereas you were speaking in October 1990.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she must have been confused. In mid-1991, direct attacks against the Yugoslav People's Army had already started, whereas the insecurities and anxiety for the people in Serb Krajina started much earlier. And I wasn't making anything up; people were fleeing already in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you visit Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1991. I believe in June or maybe -- I think it was June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the rallies? You said you went to the rallies to calm the spirits town. Who organised those rallies in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the organiser of the particular one that the lady quoted from was a party led by my former colleague from the university, Professor Novak Kilibarda, who was the leader of that party. A lot has changed for the better since then, I must say. This people's party has changed a lot. And I also tried to diffuse tensions on many other occasions, many other rallies. I don't know who organised them all, but there were ethnic divisions and rifts. On one side there were Serbs and Montenegrins. On the other side there were Muslims and Albanians. Only a line of policemen divided them. And when I arrived, I was informed that Albanians had interrupted a Serb dance and then a Turkish dance was interrupted by the other side, and the whole situation was very confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What role did you play then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the passions were running so high that I believe Mr. Blagoje Lukic, who was a high party official, had spent all day there without any success, and when I arrived I noticed that within the building the leadership had already been divided along ethnic lines. They had started shaking each other by the lapels, and I simply didn't know what to do. I saw that there was no use relying on the local leadership. I went down the stairs to address the people. I asked them to select five among them. From another group of citizens I also asked that they select five, a group of five that they trusted, and to promise me there would be no bloodshed. When we were left alone together, I wrote down their names. There was another member of the government together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's cut the long story short, Mr. Kostic. Did you fan the flames then? Did you help the tensions rise or was it quite the contrary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told those ten selected men, and later all the people who had gathered around the building, that nobody from Podgorica or from Belgrade could bring them peace and harmony unless they find it within themselves, if they want to go on living together. That was the point of all my efforts, and I stand by that even today. And the people dispersed peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was some outstanding issues concerning the Ohrid Initiative. That's tab 20 among the binders, I believe. It was a meeting of the Yugoslav Presidency with republican presidents. What was the intention and what can we see from tab 20? Could you look at paragraph 2: "We have to stand in the way of any use of force."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We must stand against the use of force which has taken human lives and continues to do so and moves us ever further away from our vital interests. "These interests are democratic development, respect for individual and collective rights and civil liberties, the continued evolution of these, and improving the quality of life. "These interests are full equality and mutual respect for the rights of our peoples to decide themselves, with sovereignty and independence, on their own fate and the fate of Yugoslavia, as well as freedom of communication and association with the world ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those the messages of Ohrid Initiative?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the messages, and they underlie the four main principles that were accepted by the full composition of the Presidency headed by Stjepan Mesic that were proclaimed at the inaugural session of The Hague peace conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how did it come about that Mesic walked out of that session of the Presidency which he chaired?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was Mesic who walked out. I think it was only Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why did he do that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was all happening in the evening, around 8.00 p.m., and Tudjman allegedly received information that there was war going on in Croatia, that there was some skirmishes, that the Yugoslav People's Army had attacked one or another area, but it was more than obvious that it was all staged. The whole attack was stage-managed to create an excuse for him to abandon the meeting in Ohrid and not to accept the Ohrid Declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there anything in that Declaration that was justified to reject?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were many things they wanted, probably, to reject but not while saving face. One of the unacceptable things for Mr. Mesic was the fact that the Declaration insisted on disarming paramilitary formations and disengagement of the Yugoslav People's Army, whereas Mesic and Tudjman always insisted that the JNA withdraw into its barracks, and that would have almost certainly led to attacks by the paramilitaries which had already been great in number against Serb areas and citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's proceed with a memorandum of understanding with the monitor mission of 1991. It exists only in English, as far as I understand. It's also one of the documents of the European Union. This seems to be a confirmation of the claim that the suspension of independence was to have been for three months rather than what you explained. Point B(1): "To monitor the suspension of the implementation of the declaration of independence for the period of three months, as agreed between the host parties -- in the --"

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 946.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "-- in Brioni --" [Interpretation] I would like the interpreters to interpret what I said, because what they interpreted was the clarification by the OTP. "[In English] -- in Brioni, particularly on the border regime and border security." [Interpretation] So they should monitor the three-month suspension, especially with regard to the border regime and border security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, could the Brioni Declaration serve as justification for any claims that suspension of independence was challenged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Its only purpose was to restore the previous condition on the borders of Yugoslavia for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those three months mentioned in the Brioni Declaration, do they refer to anybody but Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it only have to do with the Slovenian part of the Yugoslav border?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the border regime, with the suggestion or the expectation that an agreed solution would be found in the meantime, in those three months, that would be more in line with the arrangements sought by the European Community to move that role to the border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in connection with the immediate threat of war, I'm not going to dwell on that, but did you see here a decision or, rather, an act from the Official Gazette of Yugoslavia which you signed with respect to the assessment made that there was an imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having signed a document of that kind and that that was the evaluation of the 1st of October session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the stance taken. But until I had a look, I didn't remember having signed an act of that kind nor did I know that the Official Gazette had published it. But, yes, that was the evaluation that was made, and I think that is something that is so clear that we needn't go into it to prove it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what was published or, rather, the statement published, where it says that the country was facing an imminent threat of war - and that's to be found in tab 33 of the exhibits here, tab 33 in this binder of yours that has the exhibits - tell me, please, in view of the practice that the Presidency followed, do you happen to remember whether the Presidency ever published any kind of statement which was not okayed by all the members of the Presidency having discussed it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that quite certainly, and I think the Trial Chamber will also be able to see that and has seen it, because during the examination we had, for example, the stenographic notes from one of the sessions or, rather, from the 1st of October session, the Yugoslav state Presidency session. And at the end of those stenographic notes, you can see quite clearly that this discussion was conducted at the session of the 1st of October, that each paragraph and every word was discussed and that it said what had to be deleted from the text and so forth, and no similar appraisal was ever published in the Official Gazette, but everything that did -- that was a public announcement or public statement was something that all the Presidency members had spent time analysing and adopted by all the members. And we can see in those stenographic notes that at that particular meeting we adopted six or seven minutes from previous meetings and previous Presidency sessions, which confirms what I said earlier on, that the stenographic notes were authorised only if they were to be published publicly, and we accepted and adopted minutes at Presidency session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now let's dwell for a moment on the minutes that were shown you by the other side, and it is a draft minutes for the 144th session, held on the 3rd of October, and the first point on the agenda is: Agreement and discussion on ensuring the continuity and the work of the Presidency on the basis of an assessment made by the Yugoslav state Presidency from the 143rd session, the Presidency session of the 1st of October of the existence of imminent threat of war and moving to the -- and having the Presidency moved to working under conditions of an imminent threat of war. Do you have that document before you, those minutes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What tab is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not in a tab. It was shown you by the other side during the cross-examination, and it claims something that I want to ask you about here and now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't seem to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's Exhibit 328, tab 13. These are the minutes of the 3rd October session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it being provided to the witness? Mr. Milosevic, you should have a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have absolutely no facilities to make a copy of what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff presents here. I don't know where I would be expected to make a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the cross-examination, I did see a copy, but the copy was taken back afterwards, so I don't have it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I'll ask that my own copy be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I'll ask you my questions looking at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we are wasting time. This goes to the management of your case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just explain to me, please, Mr. Robinson, where is it that I can make a copy and provide it to the witness from the documents that the lady or, rather, the other side produced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pro se liaison officer, and she could have assisted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, have you found --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... whether it is able to show the document such as this which is in the computer already, whether they can show this document to the witness via Sanction or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Dicklich is trying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But actually, we always provide when we have here the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not to the witness but also to Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but the document which is shown to the witness has been taken back. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, yes, but Mr. Milosevic has it, and he has it now from my binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, point 1 on page 2, does it say there: "Unanimously assess that we were confronted -" and that was the 1st of October session, the Presidency session with six members -- was that the 1st of October session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Unanimously assess that we were confronted with an imminent threat of war." Imminent threat of war, of an all-out civil war, and that the country is in a state of imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was this imminent threat of war situation that the country faced? What does it say here? Threat or danger of what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of an all-out civil war on the territory, that's what it says. Because to all intents and purposes, there was already a war on in the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say in the following paragraph? Does it say that all the conditions are ripe for the Yugoslav state Presidency to work as provided for by the SFRY constitution under conditions of an imminent threat of war situation, because we were not able to convene before the 1st of October? And what does it say at the end of the paragraph? What does the president say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency of the SFRY did --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of the second paragraph, the last sentence, what does that say there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "The Presidency of the SFRY --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's on page 2. You'll find it on page 2.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, I see, on page 2. "The Presidency of the SFRY rejects the possibility of its work being blocked and takes it upon itself the competencies of the Assembly -- certain competencies of the Assembly of the SFRY Presidency because it cannot be convened."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you use any of those competencies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, although we had the power to adopt decree laws, because the Assembly had already been blocked by Slovenia and Croatia. But we did not avail ourselves of that constitutional right and we could have done so as the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, there was a lot of interest on the part of the other side during the cross-examination about the penultimate paragraph on that same page, where the following is stated: "That all members of the Presidency of the SFRY should be informed immediately." And read on: "That the Presidency of the SFRY, during the existence of --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- an imminent threat of war, will convene continuously in Belgrade and in connection to that it is necessary that the Yugoslav state Presidency should either be in Belgrade or be in close vicinity for them to be able to reconvene within the space of two hours after the session has been scheduled."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: The opposite side insisted here upon the fact that you made it impossible for certain Presidency members to come to the sessions. Now, how were they able to arrive, to attend the meetings? For example, a Presidency present from Slovenia or Macedonia or Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, how did they regularly come to attend the Presidency sessions? What means of transport? Just answer. What means of transport? Don't say what you had, just what means of transport.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aeroplanes. The Presidency had its own aircraft, small aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they come in to attend Presidency sessions always using those aircraft? Did they -- were they flown in every time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were flown in every time. They might have come by car on occasion, but they did use the 12-seater small planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, how long would it have taken them to fly to Belgrade from some of the other capitals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an hour at the utmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, one hour. Now, you said -- state here that they have to be somewhere where they can reach Belgrade within the space of two hours.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, but even without this situation of imminent threat of war, all the Presidency members were duty-bound to be in their offices in their cabinets in Belgrade, and they had their official accommodation provided in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right, but did this decision bind them and make them obliged to come into Belgrade even if they were in their own republics and own capital cities, and were they in any danger in coming to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not, because Mr. Tudjman had talks with you and Kadijevic just a few days prior to that, for example. He was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, in his book, writes that a JAT plane was placed at his disposal to take him there, to fly him in, and he still didn't turn up. That's what Mesic writes in his own book. So it's more than clear that it was an intentional attempt at blockading the Presidency, at blocking the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you have the following minutes that were presented to you here by the other side over there from the 145th session.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't seem to have that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm expecting you to conclude your re-examination by the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's tab 11. Tab 11 of Exhibit 328.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that, Mr. Kostic, before you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can read it out. The question asked here was that you assigned some decrees, because it says the Presidency president informed the Presidency of the decrees signed from the sphere of command of the armed forces. Now, to do away with all doubts and to clarify what a decree can refer to or relate to -- or let me put it this way: Is the subject of a decree issued, or can the subject of a decree be any kind of order to the army to undertake any kind of military action, military operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No orders of that kind. A decree can only be to appoint or dismiss an ambassador, for example, or to promote somebody to a higher rank, applying to top-ranking army officers, or a decree can once again be the promotion to rank of cadets after they had completed their military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Or commendations and medals; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is there any theoretical possibility that a decree can contain a military order of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We won't dwell on that any more then. Thank you. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in quoting from the stenographic notes of the 143rd session of the 1st of October, quoted the deputy federal secretary for foreign affairs, and that was on page 44, and we have a translation of it in English, and she provided it in the original and with an attached translation, where she said the following -- or, rather, where she quoted the deputy foreign minister saying that a West European Union meeting had been held and the 12 ministers for foreign affairs, and then it goes on to say, according to Maksic, they agreed on the following: To call, in a declaration that was being prepared, all the parties in Yugoslavia that after the moratorium they continue sitting on the Conference on Yugoslavia in The Hague and that they should do that with goodwill, bona fides, so as to enable the conference order to be fruitful and make the right decisions. So the other side over there suggested to you that at the time you bore in mind the fact that the moratorium would expire on independence. Now, what Maksic said, did that in any way or can that in any way relate to some expiration of a moratorium on independence? Because they said they agreed after the moratorium expired. Now, what did the moratorium relate to? And you were all aware of that, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the moratorium related to a cease-fire, to a truce, and peace so that in peaceful conditions political settlements could be found to the crisis, and not a moratorium with respect to independence. That wasn't what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, the other side over there also quoted another thing. It was Jovic's variation for the future of Yugoslavia from some kind of meeting with you and with myself. Now, can you remember or could you tell us whether that might have been from his diary, thoughts written down in his diary, or any of our own thoughts, or were they all of our thoughts together, the way we thought?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the cross-examination I said I had reservations to make with respect to a lot of things that Jovic wrote about in his book, because quite obviously, looking at several examples, we saw that it wasn't actually a diary that he kept on a regular basis but he might have shaped it into a diary much later on. Now, as far as this, I already said during the cross-examination that these were his own personal thoughts but that all our thoughts together about the different variants and solutions moved along the direction of preserving the reduced Yugoslavia as it was, and that was what the convention for Yugoslavia of the 3rd of January also came out in favour of. So we really didn't expect a conflict in Bosnia to break out between the Muslims and Serbs until the very last moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, here you were also shown a declaration by the European Union, or rather it was the European Community at the time, about the situation in Yugoslavia, with claims that it was confirmation of the fact that Carrington's plan was adopted in advance, accepted in advance. And that is why a quotation was chosen from Momir Bulatovic's book. Now, this is a very important matter, so I'm going to ask you a few questions in that regard, and they are these: On page 2 of this declaration about the situation in Yugoslavia, the 28th of October 1991, which was drafted in Brussels -- no, I do apologise. This doesn't seem to be it. There was another document from the European Union. Let me just take a moment to find it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it could be Exhibit 812, the Conference on Yugoslavia Summary of Developments that I used quite a lot, so I assume that Mr. Milosevic refers to this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to find the document of the European Union which mentions what van den Broek stated after the meeting that was held. I had it here. But as it's identical or similar to what is in Mr. Bulatovic's book, I will use the book. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this. It's page 65, page 65 of Momir Bulatovic's book, which you were shown here. It says: "The basis of this solution, as the document said, will be independence to those republics that want it at the end of the talks, which are to be held bona fide." This is on the 4th of October. Lord Carrington and Hans van den Broek accepted this, and it goes on to say: "The independence will be granted on the basis --" or, rather: "Independence will be granted to those republics that want it at the end of the talks, which are to be held bona fide." At any point in time did the Presidency of SFRY or Serbia or Montenegro deny the right to any people in Yugoslavia who wanted to to secede?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for a single moment. We never challenged this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it our standpoint that this should happen at the end of a negotiating process which was meant to protect everybody's rights?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our standpoint was that in the search for political solutions and in the negotiations, all options should be considered equally, that an agreement should be reached through a political process. Our side, which was advocating the Yugoslav option, insisted that just as the peoples and republics had an equal right to secession, those republics who wanted to stay in Yugoslavia and continue living together had at least an equal right. We never denied the right to secession. All those republics who wanted to secede were denying the right of us who were remaining in Yugoslavia to have our place in The Hague conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if van den Broek said that a solution should be found, bearing in mind that those republics who wanted to secede would be able to secede, but it says here at the end of the talks. Does it say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the same thing that we were saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So was anybody denying this or bringing it into question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were such negotiations held or were they interrupted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were interrupted after the 5th of November when the seceding republics rejected what Mr. Carrington was already prepared to include in the first chapter of The Hague document, and that is that those republics that wanted to stay in Yugoslavia had to be treated on an equal footing and given the same rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when was that meeting in The Hague held where I refused or rejected the Carrington paper?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly two weeks after this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As it says here that all this was to take place at the end of the talks which are to be held bona fide, was it possible 14 days later to declare that Yugoslavia no longer exists?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could that have been the end of bona fide negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you were given a quotation from the book of Smilja Avramov. I received only one page of that, and then it's interrupted, but it says here that I said that we could not accept the offered solutions to the Yugoslav crisis because practically this was abolishing Yugoslavia, a state that had existed for 70 years, and that an international forum could not issue a decision on abolishing a country, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have appended this, Mr. Robinson, and you can read it. As an international lawyer, I don't believe you can have any objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the first point of the Carrington paper, was it that Yugoslavia ceases to exist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is stated here, that independence would be achieved at the end of talks which are to be held bona fide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, stop. You've been asking leading questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The answers are worthless.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, what is quoted from the documents is not worthless, I assume, Mr. Robinson, regardless of whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the documents are in evidence. I had indicated that I expected you to finish your re-examination by the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be very difficult for me to conclude by the end of this session, but I'm doing my best and skipping over many questions, which I'm trying to reduce to a minimum, but I certainly won't be finished by the end of this session. That's now, as far as I can see. Let's just finish with this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say here? "Independence to those republics that want it at the end of the talks which are to be held bona fide." Were there any talks after that 4th of October? This document is dated the 4th of October. Were there any talks after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th and then on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute, wait a minute. This was written on the 4th of October. Were there any talks after the 4th of October and before the 18th of October when it was proposed that Yugoslavia be abolished? Were there any talks in the intervening period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say because I didn't participate in them, but I think there were some talks. I'm not sure exactly when or where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, if you can say nothing about it, but would it have been possible for talks to have been completed within 14 days, ending in a proposal that Yugoslavia be abolished, on the basis of what it says here, at the end of the talks which are to be held bona fide?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during my previous testimony I said that the principle of seeking a political solution, taking everybody's rights equally into account, were diverged from in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. You have tab 2 here where you had that long conversation. What was your aim when you had this conversation with the representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? Just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our main goal was to convince the leadership of the Republika Srpska Krajina to accept the peace plan of Cyrus Vance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read what it says on page 34. This is a fast dialogue.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Branko Kostic --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, Paspalj finishes. What does he say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Now, this part of the people who dare to defend first themselves --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Read slowly because the interpreters are slow.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Now, that part of the people who dare to defend first themselves to save the honour of the remainder of Yugoslavia, the army, these people we are putting under the patronage of the United Nations and in some way leaving to it to its own fate, to what the world powers decide."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So leaving them to their fate and to the decision of the world powers. Paspalj, the president of the Assembly, says this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I reply: "Why did the conflict break out there? Why was there a military conflict in the Krajina?" Paspalj says: "That's clear to everyone." I ask: "I'm asking you why. Is it because the Croatian authorities attempted on that territory to impose their own authority over you? Is that correct?" Paspalj says: "Correct." I say: "And you rose up and organised yourselves to defend yourselves against it." Mile Paspalj: "We defended ourselves." Branko Kostic: "You defended yourselves."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, we were looking at page 34 of the shorthand notes, and you say: "Why did conflict erupt in Krajina? Is it because the Croatian authorities tried to impose their authority and power on this territory; is that right? You rose and organised yourselves to defend yourselves from against this." And he says: "We have defended ourselves." This quick, spontaneous exchange, does it really indicate what happened there or does it indicate something else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are original shorthand notes. They're contemporaneous, they were not prepared for anyone else, including this Tribunal, and they only go to support what I said during my testimony. This is precisely what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The other side here, in connection with the Convention on Yugoslavia, showed you certain maps which turned out to be UNPROFOR maps showing the demographic break-up of the Yugoslav map. At the convention on the new Yugoslavia, were there any maps, either that map or anything similar to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, there were no maps at the convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any discussion of borders at that convention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the convention and during the discussion, all that was mentioned was that we should all come together regardless of our differences to preserve Yugoslavia as our common state and that this Yugoslavia should be based on principles acceptable to all; that is, the equality of all peoples and all republics, leaving open the possibility of later accession. The Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina saw it as their vital interest to preserve Yugoslavia. When they saw they couldn't, they accepted independent Bosnia, but an independent Bosnia where there would be no predominance, where all peoples would have equal rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In their cross-examination, the other side showed you your book, page 179, drawing attention to footnote 85 at the bottom of that page. Please take a look at that as well as the following page, and I'll put a question to you in this respect.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: She drew your attention to footnote 85, and you say: "The decision of the Presidency of the SFRY on the withdrawal of JNA units from territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been fully implemented by then."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interview given to ZDF, the German broadcasting company, and this was in June, whereas on the 18th or 19th of May, we had already withdrawn all JNA units from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, now for footnote 86 on the following page, not shown to you by the other side, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The leadership of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially Dr. Radovan Karadzic, pointed out more than once that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina are handicapped in relation to the Muslims and the Croats because the JNA was recruiting a large part of their manpower, whereas the other sides were -- and they were -- the JNA was acting with extreme restraint, whereas the other two sides were very aggressive."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does this show?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It shows what I constantly kept pointing out, that the JNA was acting with extreme restraint on all the territories where it was positioned, and it also confirms what I have already stated, that the Muslims and the Croats stopped sending their recruits to the JNA and that they, rather, sent them to their own paramilitary formations. At the same time, it denies what Mr. Jovic said, that I said I would never subscribe to the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I want you to read that. That's the next quotation. But what you have just said about not sending Muslim recruits to the JNA, did Izetbegovic confirm this at your meeting in Skopje? Are we able to see this on that stenogram, on those shorthand notes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that the Muslim leadership in Bosnia bore part of the responsibility for the fact that the JNA had become the army of a single nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you write in the next footnote?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The immediate decision on the withdrawal of the JNA just before the decision was reached to withdraw the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I said in public, in a speech, I quoted: "I will never subscribe to the withdrawal of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina without the prior agreement of all three leaderships of that republic. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, composed of the most responsible representatives of the Croats and Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially requested the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is my impression that the leadership of the Serbian people could hardly wait for this. We had talks with Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, and Dr. Nikola Koljevic, at which we gained their agreement to the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Later on, my political opponents often accused me of making that statement, but they only quoted the first half, not the other half of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the other half was that you would never subscribe to it without the agreement of all three leaderships.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you gained their agreement because the Croats and Muslims had agreed to it and Karadzic and Koljevic in their conversation with you also agreed to it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did you act in accordance with your stated position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The side opposite gave you a map related -- I don't know what's written here. A map depicting evidence, crime base evidence, reflected in the indictment. Now, look, I have only a couple of questions in this regard. Do you have the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take it, and we can also put it on the overhead projector if it's suitable. Now, please, look, on the territory of Serbia is there a single act of murder according to this map, which is a graphic depiction of their evidence? Is there a single killing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this map, no, no single crime on the territory of Serbia, including murders. And what there is is concentrated in the border area between Croatia and Serbia and in the border areas between Serbia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a single murder in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the percentage of non-Serb population in Serbia then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 34 per cent. More than one-third.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So over 3 million, 3.5 million.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And none of them were affected?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the blue points. They show detentions. As you can see, in four places in Serbia detentions are indicated, places of detention.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five: Lovac, Sremska Mitrovica, Sid --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lovac is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, out of those four places, is there a single one under the authority of Serbia? Look from the top. Begici - paragraph 64(e) - JNA barracks. Is that what's written? And then: Stajicevo agricultural complex, JNA. Then Sid military prison, JNA. Sremska Mitrovica military prison, JNA. Is that it?
