utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a single prison that was run by Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at Montenegro. There is Morinje, also a military depot of the JNA. Are there any prisons, places of detention run by Montenegrin authorities?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All these military installations belong to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened, to the best of your knowledge, with the people who were detained there, and who were those people anyway?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were prisoners, members of Croatian paramilitaries who were taken prisoner by the JNA and detained in those places. Later, a number of them were exchanged. I mentioned Dr. Vesna Bosanac, who used to be the director of the Vukovar Hospital. She was indicted before Serbian courts as a war criminal. But even she was later exchanged during that exchange conducted by Mr. Banic on the principle of all for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody murdered in those prisons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a pretty voluminous document sent by the Helsinki Watch. Is it in any way different from this map? Does it show anything in existence in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you received a letter from the Helsinki Watch sent to me and Blagoje Adzic speaking of violations of human rights, and they go on to enumerate places like Strugar, Dvor, Benkovac, Osijek, Lovinac near Gracac, Petrinje, Belinci in Podravska Slatina, Gospic, Grubisno Polje, Bogdanovci, and so on. Is there a single place there that is located in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They're all in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Regarding Dubrovnik, what were we all told by the top military echelons concerning Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The top military leaders responded to all our warnings and requests first by informing us that their troops on the ground had strict orders not to come close to the Old Town, not to come within the range of any forces that might be located in the Old Town. They also had strict orders not to shell or bomb Dubrovnik, to preserve the Old Town. And I must say that we were kept informed about this. It is also true that propaganda was very vociferous on both sides, especially the Croatian propaganda saying that the entire Dubrovnik was about to be destroyed. I already mentioned that there is another place, called Cavtat, near Dubrovnik where JNA troops entered without firing a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What's important to me is this: What was the JNA answer to our questions about what was going on in Dubrovnik, why it was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that it was Croatian propaganda, that the Old Town was not being shelled, that they had information that many vital buildings in the Old Town had mines and explosives planted around them, that Croatian forces were staging certain attacks in order to blame the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did we have a single piece of information telling us that the JNA was really shelling Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We requested information. What was the answer; that they were shelling or they were not shelling?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer was that Dubrovnik was not being shelled. And even in the case of the 6th of December, about which I learned the most from the trial before this Tribunal, the naval base of the JNA informed us and the general public that there was no shelling of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to ask, where would that information have come from that the JNA was not shelling Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received our information from the most responsible, the highest-ranking people of the Supreme Command Staff with whom we kept in touch. I didn't communicate with commanders on the ground, we communicated with Generals Adzic, Kadijevic, and Brovet, whereas the official information came from the Military-Naval Sector of Boka, and it was published as an official communique refuting allegations in the Croatian press, in propaganda, that there was a particularly bad shelling on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, these are very general answers that you're giving about this, but the impression I have is that you would actually be face-to-face with someone who held a senior position in the army, who would tell you what was happening in Dubrovnik. Can you tell us who principally gave you the information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Bonomy, I visited those troops, those units, for about two or three hours. Of course I was unable to visit Dubrovnik itself because there were military conflicts going on. I visited the environs of Dubrovnik, and the commanders with whom we talked on the spot told us that certain buildings and even the walls of the Old Town were being used as firing points. And during cross-examination, I also said that I had had the opportunity to see some footage and documentaries from which I was able to see that there had been shelling of Dubrovnik and some buildings had been destroyed, but it was not on such a massive scale as the propaganda was trying to represent at the time, and still today I would say that there was no such destruction of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that, but in an earlier part of the -- the reason I ask this question, you earlier said, "I didn't communicate with commanders on the ground." At least, that's the translation in the transcript. And you mentioned the most senior personnel, Adzic, Kadijevic, and Brovet. But you now say that you actually got the information from commanders on the ground at Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, the Dubrovnik operation lasted for several months, and that information that we received regarding the Dubrovnik operation and everything else came to us regularly from the very top, from the Supreme Command Staff. And this was an individual visit that lasted two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the main information was received from the Supreme Command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Among these documents, some of which have been shown here, and I mean the documents related to JNA decisions in attachment 123, there is a letter by Kadijevic to Mr. van den Broek of the 4th of November, 1991, where he says: "Connecting to the military actions in the area of Dubrovnik, I emphasise the following facts: JNA units have received many strict orders not to fire on the Old Town of Dubrovnik under any circumstances, even if the Old Town is being used as a firing position." That was written by Kadijevic to van den Broek on the 4th of November, 1991. Was that the same thing that Kadijevic kept telling you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was some dispute about a certain document which was a warning of the Supreme Command Staff to the Republic of Croatia, its president and the headquarters of the Main Staff of the Croatian army. You found that document. Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please read just the last paragraph, because there were -- there are two points here. In the other one, there were four points. What is authentic, the one with two points or the one with four points?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have given a copy to the ladies and gentlemen of the Prosecution. I'm not sure I have another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think way are dealing with 948, but before that, Mr. Milosevic, I didn't follow what documents you were referring to when you said the JNA decisions in attachment 123.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, is that a question to me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. 123 is an attachment from the same collection to which Exhibit 948 belongs. Its number is 87, whereas 123 is a letter from Kadijevic to Mr. van den Broek of the 4th of November, 1991. I quoted from it the passage where he informs van den Broek that several strict orders had been issued not to fire on Dubrovnik under any circumstances, which is the same information we received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think so, but as I understand the tabs that we have in binder 2 of Mr. Milosevic, are all from a collection I think prepared from the JNA, and I'm not sure that this document number 123 is part of it. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be clarified later on. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I can give you that document. It's absolutely identical to the ones we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So have you received the one that you had found yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It has two points, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say after those two points? "If you wish to avoid bloodshed and destruction, let the local authorities immediately get in touch --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... let [them] immediately get in touch with the competent JNA commands in order to enable absolutely safe passage for withdrawing units with their movable property as well as the families of JNA members from the jeopardised garrisons. International monitors can be engaged too."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this warning from the Supreme Command Staff, was it a threat?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this should be considered as a warning. If the Croatian authorities cut off the water, electricity, telephone lines, and food supplies to 125.000 JNA members -- sorry, 25.000, and prevent them from taking out their wounded and even dead to be buried, I suppose that even today in the same circumstances, after ten attempts at cease-fire that had not been observed, I would write such a warning myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this threat realised in all these garrisons that had been under attack?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was understood as a threat. To what purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a warning to finally persuade Croatian paramilitaries and Croatian authorities to finally accept something that they had already pretended to accept in all the previous cease-fire agreements, to enable the withdrawal of our JNA members and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. Your book, "Lest it be Forgotten," was presented to you, page 108, a passage referring to the pensioning off of generals. You spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason underlying the reduction of the number of generals?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that even then, in peacetime conditions, for the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia we already had an excessive number of generals that was unusually high for the general number of the army. In the meantime, wars erupted, Croatia and Slovenia stopped sending their recruits, followed by Kosovo Albanians, followed by Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslims in Bosnia. The territory of Yugoslavia, although it still existed as a legitimate state, was halved, and it was normal to reduce that number of generals that had been too high even in peacetime. And we were the Supreme Command, competent for those issues, and we still sought approval, and we sought a list of all generals of the JNA from the General Staff, broken down by various branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did I play any role in that job that you just described?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, really not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did I intervene, asking to pension off or not to pension off any single general?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said you didn't intervene about anybody. You didn't even call me. The only conversation we had on the subject was a pretty angry comment you made concerning Mr. Marko Negovanovic, who was your Serbian minister of defence, and you hadn't even been informed that he would be pensioned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did I say on that occasion? Did I protest because he was being pensioned off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You protested because you said it would have been normal to at least inform you, seeing how he was the president -- sorry, the minister of defence of Serbia. And I explained that he was not being pensioned off as the minister of defence, he was being pensioned off as head of the 12th administration of the army counter-intelligence, and that he was the most responsible for the -- the whole thing in Slovenia, together with Aleksandar Vasiljevic. At the time when the Slovenian operation took place, he was head of the 12th administration of the army counter-intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say at least something after ten days without being asked any questions by you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No; we don't like volunteers. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just to clarify something you said a short time ago when you were referred to your book and the speech you made about the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia, and you said: "The Presidency of Bosnia, composed of the most responsible representatives of the Croats and Muslims, officially requested the withdrawal of the JNA. It is my impression that the leadership of the Serbian people could hardly wait for this." What did you mean by that sentence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's actually explained in the book, but maybe I failed to remind you of something that we have discussed even during my evidence. The leadership of the Serbian people in Bosnia constantly complained that the engagement of their recruits and military men in the JNA was weakening their position as representatives of the Serbian people in that territory under the circumstances when the Croats and Muslims already had established their paramilitary units. And with the withdrawal of the JNA, all the Serb members of the JNA who were natives of Bosnia would be free to join the Serbian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, thus strengthening the Serbian position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now understand the point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, that concludes your evidence, and thank you for coming to give it at the Tribunal. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one issue in relation to exhibits. I had used this map that the Office of the Prosecutor made with the witness, but I actually only used it as a visual aid, but as now Mr. Milosevic also used it, I wonder whether we should exhibit it. It's just depicting -- it's just depicting the crime bases, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's illustrative of the Prosecution's case rather than being an exhibit that derives from the witness and should be part of their final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It has more the character of an aide-memoire than an exhibit. The next witness -- Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness comes in, there is a couple of administrative matters that I'd be grateful to deal with. It will only take a couple of minutes. The first is just a general observation that we are still working on a witness list that is really one witness at a time. We're getting notification of one witness at a time and always uncertainty as to future witnesses. The second matter, could we have a couple of minutes in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are in public session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there was a matter raised in public session, I think, by Mr. Nice about the witness Mr. Bulatovic. You were to inform us -- that was in private session? It was in private session. Let us return to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you're also to provide more information on your witness list, and I would say for the next four to six weeks. You should provide the Chamber and the parties your witnesses for that period. May we have the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you may begin your examination-in-chief, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Atlagic, would you please introduce yourself in brief terms.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Marko Atlagic. I was born on the 30th of April, 1949, in the village of Ostrovica, Benkovac municipality. I completed primary school in Ostrovica, after which I went to secondary school for the teachers training course in Benkovac. After completing secondary school, I enrolled at the faculty of philosophy in Zadar to study history and pedagogy, and after that I went on to do my post-graduate studies at the same university, for historical sciences. I received an M.A., a Ph.D., and now I'm professor at the faculty of philosophy in Pristina, with headquarters in Kosovska Mitrovica. My first job was at the primary school in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's quite clear that the witness has in front of him and appears to be reading from what looks like a prepared list of notes or a statement. Such a pity it wasn't served under 89(F) to save time if prepared in typed form, as would appear to be the case. But I know the Chamber likes to know whether witnesses are referring to notes, and if so what, and then to decide whether they're available to the Prosecution to review.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone be adjusted as well, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please have the witness's microphone adjusted. And, Mr. Atlagic, I'm to ask you, are you reading from a document? Are you reading from a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying now I'm not reading from documents, but I have prepared general theses in front of me. And you may feel free to take a look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. When did you prepare this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I prepared them over the last two or three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, yes. I think we have the background information. Do you want any more background information?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll ask him about any more background information that I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, what posts did you occupy? What positions in Croatia during 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: From 1990 to 1992, I was the deputy in the Assembly of the Sabor in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what elections were you elected to the parliament of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I was elected to the parliament of Croatia at elections held in 1990, the first multi-party elections that were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On whose party's ticket? Which party put you forward for member of the Croatian Sabor or parliament?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I was on the list of the Alliance of Socialists of Croatia, and I was elected deputy to the Croatian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That particular party, ethnically speaking was it a uni-ethnic party or a multi-ethnic party? What was the ethnic composition of the party in whose name your name was nominated for deputy?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the party was as follows: We had deputies who were both Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a Serb or a Croat at the head of the party?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Zeljko Mazar, a Croat, headed the party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one thing missing from the transcript about your current position. Did you say you were a professor in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And professor of what subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Historical sciences at the department of philosophy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that during that critical time, that is to say 1990 to 1992, you were a member of parliament or, rather, a member of the Croatian Sabor as it's called, what was your electoral base from which you went to represent the citizens in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, my base was Benkovac, the Benkovac municipality. My constituency was Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that critical point in time did you have numerous contacts with your constituency and all the information coming in to you about what was going on in the area from which you were elected by the population to the Croatian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did have information from the constituency, as far as a deputy can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have all information about events going on in the Croatian Assembly whose member you were about the subject matter discussed, the political situation and so on?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did have information about the topics under discussion in the Croatian Assembly, and I think I was an active participation in the discussions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you actively participated as a member of the Croatian parliament; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I acquitted myself with honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of your function and post and the fact that you were politically active throughout in the Republic of Croatia, tell us the following, please. I'm going ask you a question which is raised in point 6 of the indictment, for example, where a joint criminal enterprise is referred to on our part; that is to say that I myself was the person who organised it there, the purpose of which was the forcible removal of the majority of the Croats and other non-Serb population from the approximately one-third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia, that I planned to become part of a new Serb-dominated state through the commission of crimes, et cetera, et cetera. Now, as you were a politician throughout that time, an actor on the political arena, what can you tell us about that time in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: There was no joint criminal enterprise in which you, Milosevic, took part, and therefore you could not have forcibly removed the non-Serb population from the territory of the Republic of Croatia by the same token or -- nor could you have planned it to become part of the new Serb-dominated state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is the truth, then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: The truth is quite different: That had a joint criminal enterprise existed -- or, rather, that Franjo Tudjman was the head of the joint criminal enterprise that existed, the president of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the purpose of what you qualify as joint criminal enterprise on the part of the Croatian leadership? What was its purpose?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of that leadership was to break up the Federal Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia in order to create an Independent State of Croatia without any Serbs, and the legal continuity of this would have been an appendage to the Fascist Independent State of Croatia, a state from World War II, which would incorporate today's Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Bay of Kotor and Backa including Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say at the head, now, as you were a representative in the Croatian Assembly, who was the head of creating that Croatia without Serbs? Who else was involved in that enterprise for you to be able to testify about it as an Assembly member who saw this acted out?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of heads, a number of leaders in the Republic of Croatia. Among others, Dr. Zarko Domljan, the president of the Croatian Assembly and president of the Executive Council of the Republic of Croatia; Josip Manolic, the vice-president of the Croatian Assembly; Sulimanac, Stjepan Sulimanac; and the second vice-president of Croatia, Vladimir Seks; the minister of the interior of the Republic of Croatia, Josip Boljkovac; and Martin Spegelj, minister of defence; as well as member of the SFRY Presidency and later president of the Yugoslav state Presidency who is the present day president, Mr. Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On what basis do you claim that they were involved at that time, that is to say when you were a deputy or, rather, member of parliament in creating a Croatia without the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the general atmosphere and, later, all the events that took place in at that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a document stating that this was actually the aim? You are speaking on the basis of your experience.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the party platform of the Croatian Democratic Union, especially the provisions of the first general convention and the statements issued by the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the convention of the Croatian Democratic Union and its decisions. Are these decisions of the first party convention in tab 1?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at tab 1 and tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Tab 1 contains the decisions from the first general convention of the HDZ, the party platform, the statute, and so on. On page 39, in the lower left-hand corner, it says that the HDZ will advocate the current inalienable right to self-determination of the Croatian nation within their historical and natural borders. Croatia is mentioned within its natural and historical borders. These are the borders I mentioned at the outset. That's today's Republic of Croatia, plus Bosnia-Herzegovina, plus Boka Kotorska, plus Srem and Backa, as well as Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this something new on the Croatian political scene? Was this something new that emerged only in the 1990s and was espoused by the main leader, Franjo Tudjman, or was this something that can be found in previous historical periods?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: No. This was nothing new. Dr. Tudjman had advocated these ideas previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you support this with an example?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1964, Dr. Franjo Tudjman wrote that he was advocating Croatia and its historical and natural borders. By this he was implying the AVNOJ Croatia, plus Bosnia-Herzegovina, plus Boka Kotorska, plus Srem and Backa with Subotica. And for this reason he was interrogated before the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you are speaking about now, is it contained in the document in tab 3 where there is a book by two authors entitled "The Croats and Bosnia." Look at tab 3. I hope you have this before you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do have tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let it be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please put page 69 on the ELMO. We have a very brief quotation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's 96 in the text which we have, Mr. Milosevic, not 69.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 96, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is quoted here from Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I will try to read out what Dr. Tudjman said. "From the Historical Borders of Croatia (the tripartite kingdom of Croatia), Srem and Boka Kotorska were taken away and Srem and Boka Kotorska were not added to it which was part of Croatia before, and parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srem and Backa with Subotica were left out also."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of those who are looking at this and who are not familiar with the geography, could you explain where these territories are and these places that are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina is the neighbouring republic. However, Boka Kotorska is in the Republic of Montenegro, whereas Backa, including Subotica, is in the Republic of Serbia, in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about Srem? Where is Srem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Srem is in Serbia partly, and a part of it is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because in paragraph 7 of the indictment, it claims that this joint criminal enterprise came into existence before the 1st of August, 1991, tell us, what was the situation in Croatia before the 1st of August, 1991? To be more precise, what was the situation as regards the multi-party elections in which you were elected and after the HDZ won the elections and came into power with Dr. Franjo Tudjman at its head?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the multi-party elections, the Croatian Democratic Union celebrated its victories. In almost every village they roast bulls on spits, and then, half drunk in the evening hours, people would pass through Serbian hamlets, provoking the Serbian population by singing various songs, calling on the names of Ante Pavelic and Ante Starcevic. The authorities did not respond to this. Slogans emerged, slogans against the Serbs, on kiosks and on the facades of buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did this campaign and this atmosphere you're describing start, these slogans and all the rest?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: It was in 1989 that these slogans first began to turn up, but later on they became more frequent. In the 1990s, when the HDZ came into power, they became ubiquitous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the slogans that predominated in public?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were many of them. The most frequent ones were: "Hang the Serbs from willow trees," "We shall slaughter Serbs, sons of whores," and things like that. "We shall expel the Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the authorities react to these slogans and graffiti?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: The authorities did not react at all in the period leading up to 1992. The authorities ignored this. They considered it quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For you Serbs and for you as a member of parliament in the parliament of Croatia, what did this attitude of the authorities in Croatia signify in 1990, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: To the Serbs in Croatia and us who were in the government, it signified a restoration of Croatia and its so-called historical borders, also a Croatia devoid of Serbs. They called on the name of Ante Starcevic, who was the greatest Serb-later in the entire history of Croat-Serb relations. This man had said that the Serbs did not exist, not just in Croatia but also in Serbia. He called them Gypsies, Vuljaks [phoen], Balkan riffraff. He thought that the Serbs as a political nation did not exist at all, only the Croats. He uttered a well-known sentence that the Croats were the only political nation in Croatia and that the Serbs were part of those people; that is, that they didn't exist as such. The Serbs were very upset by all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please be kind enough to look into tab 2 where we have a quotation from a very eminent Croatian intellectual, Joza Horvat. This is a very brief quotation. It can be put on the ELMO. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page is it, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 97, a brief quotation. Here it is on the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say here, Mr. Atlagic? Please read it. This is what the prominent Croatian intellectual Joza Horvat said about these activities. Now, please, you read the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: "Not a little fear and incredulity was introduced by the propaganda agitation of the HDZ. After winning the elections, they fiercely set upon all the traces of the people's liberation struggle. Our President Franjo Tudjman, not as a general but as an historian, should explain it to us ignoramuses the following: Had there not been the people's liberation struggle, had there not been Tito and the Partizans, there would be no present-day Republic of Croatia or the HDZ."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a Croatian intellectual responding to this atmosphere and all these events. Calling upon the names of Pavelic and Starcevic, which you mentioned, could this leave the Serbs in any doubt as to what was in store for them, what this meant for them? Could there have been any doubt among them?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I haven't yet objected to the book, I'm not sure what value that's going to have, the assertion as to who this person is, but even so, even if the book is admissible, the next question isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the question is -- is leading. I'll allow you to reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were slogans on the political scene and that the names of Pavelic and Starcevic were invoked. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As we are now discussing ideas and slogans, my question is as follows: Were these ideas implemented or did they begin to be implemented in practice in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. In the 1990s, they began to be put into practice, and this is how: The president of the republic, Franjo Tudjman, in almost every one of his speeches, invoked the name of Ante Starcevic, calling him the father of the homeland, ignoring Starcevic's attitude to the Serbs. And of course this could not leave the Serbs indifferent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this quotation that you read just a minute ago, you -- because I don't want to put a leading question -- you touched upon anti-fascism. In the new HDZ government, what was typical for their attitude towards anti-Fascism?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: The new HDZ government was characterised first of all by their denial of the fighters of the anti-fascist movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some examples?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, the new authorities renamed the Victims of Fascism Square in Zagreb and called it Mile Budak Square.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who is Mile Budak?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: He was the head of the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945. He was in the Croatian government and he said that one-third of the Serbs had to be expelled, one-third had to be killed, and one-third had to be rebaptised to become Catholics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when this -- did this renaming of the Victims of Fascism Square occur?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: This happened in the period up to 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you have any other examples? You're talking about the Ustasha movement. Was there a party that openly espoused these ideas?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The new authorities, sometime in March 1991, permitted the founding of an Ustasha party in Hotel Marijan in Split. This means that they were turning their backs on everything that the fighters of the anti-fascist movement and World War II had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We're going to break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, you were speaking about that atmosphere. How did the Serbs experience it? How did you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: We were living in great fear, both Serbs and myself as an MP, because we were witnessing all that was going on, the invocations of the past and Ante Starcevic who had said that Serbs did not exist at all, that they were fit only to be axed down. So it was all inspiring great fear and misgivings among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the official position with the Croatian leadership?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: It was headed by Dr. Franjo Tudjman. He was the one who charted the policy of the Croatian leadership, and his position was that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should be broken up and an Independent State of Croatia created, and that independent state would be actually the legal successor of the criminal Independent State of Croatia from the World War II. However, that former Independent State of Croatia was under foreign control. He was invoking, however, in 1990, Ante Starcevic as the father of the homeland, and he was also invoking Ante Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We quoted from tab 3 and 2 in part. Was something particular happening in 1989, 1990, 1991 in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: By that time in 1990, and even earlier, in 1989, Franjo Tudjman attended a Conference of the Diplomatic Corps in Germany and he presented his solution for the Serb people in Krajina. He said he would resolve that issue very quickly, but he said the ground would be red with blood in Krajina. And then there are some other statements from 1990. Speaking at the Jelacic Square, he said, "Who started the war?" And he said whether it could have been avoided. He said it could have been avoided, but it was carried out nevertheless. And he also explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have tab 4 now. There is an article there called "The Nationalists are Stewing in Their Own Broth." And on page 3 of this collection of documents, we have a statement from Tudjman from 1989. Is that what you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it. I will try to quote this announcement made by Tudjman. He says: "'My experience is not so fresh as Warren's, and it comes mainly from service in Bulgaria,' emphasised Fischer. 'However, two situations that I've experienced were a drastic warning that the situation in Yugoslavia was much more complex than it had seemed to me. I remember the Conference of the Diplomatic Corps in Germany in 1989 that was attended by the future Croatian president, Tudjman. He emphasised on that occasion that when he becomes president of Croatia, the ground in Krajina will be red with blood. At that time, I didn't understand that there is a political hatred that has to emerge sooner or later. "'Another situation had to do with the meeting of the American Committee for Security and Foreign Affairs and a delegation of the European Community in October 1991 in the White House. I addressed an American politician at the time with a question: What was the position of the US concerning the crisis in Yugoslavia? and he answered, Let those fools stew in their own broth. I didn't know whether to understand it as a joke or a position reflecting the poverty of the American foreign policy.'" That is a quotation from Warren Zimmermann's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is speaking there? Whose words were you quoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zimmerman -- David Fischer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who, sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] David Fischer, speaking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is David Fischer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a politician, a German official who had served in Bulgaria for a while, as far as I know

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A German official. He's a diplomat, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He quotes here the passage where Tudjman said in 1989 that the soil in Krajina would be red with blood, and you mentioned also his speech in 1992, on the 24th of May, at Jelacic Square. Is that in tab 5?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. That quotation is under tab 5. I quote: "There would have been no war if Croatia hadn't wanted it. However, we estimated that only by war can we gain the independence for Croatia. That is why we carried on with a policy of negotiations, but behind the scenes of the negotiations, we were establishing our armed units. If we hadn't done it that way, we would not have reached our goal. Therefore, the war was possible to avoid if only we had given up on our objectives, that is, the independence of our state."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's what he stated publicly at a rally.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other messages sent out publicly that inspired fear among the Serbs and made them self-organise or respond in any way?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were many other causes for fear. Not all of them were statements, but these statements did have a great impact, not only on Serbs but also on the Croatian part of the population that was anti-fascist. There were many statements made by Croatian officials and politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at what Gerard Baudson wrote in his book called "The Europe of Fools or The Break-up of Yugoslavia." There is just a short passage that I wish to quote.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Which tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 6. Have you found page 60?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is written in the last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I quote: "Before his election into the Presidency of the republic in 1990, he publicly rejoiced over the fact that his wife was neither Serb nor Jewish. There is nothing democratic about this man. In 1989, he published a book in Zagreb titled "The Impassable Roads of Historical Reality," which can be translated as "The Flight of Historical Truth," or even better, "An Impasse of Historical Truth."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did you understand that statement such as the joy that his wife was neither Serb nor Jewish?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we were astonished, and he said to a journalist called Tanja Torbarina, "I'm really happy that my wife is neither Jewish nor Serb." We understood it as complete madness. We thought the situation from 1941 was coming back all over again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look at another passage from tab 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who is the author of tab 6?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 6? The author is Gerard Baudson, a Frenchman who wrote a book called "The Europe of Fools or The Break-up of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What are you seeking to establish with this evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm seeking to establish how this whole atmosphere was created. The witness is speaking to a fear that was obviously not groundless. It was based on political behaviour, mass behaviour, everything that was going on in Croatia even before the elections in 1991. It's a very ugly attitude towards the Serb population, the revamping of the Ustasha movement from the Second World War and public statements made by the most prominent Croat politicians, followed by self-organisation of the Serbs and their response. So I'm trying to establish a causal link, because the indictment speaks about criminal enterprise in Serbia, whereas Serbs were reacting to the situation in Croatia. And whatever action they took, it was always a response only, and those were facts of life obvious to everybody at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So this background is -- will be consistent with your case that the Serbs were always responding. Yes, continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What is written in this last paragraph on page 10, tab 7?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, I quote: "When way back in 1997 Franjo Tudjman was submitting a report to the parliament of Croatia, his state of the nation speech, he mentioned as the greatest achievement of his policy the disappearance of Serbs from Croatia and the fact that they were reduced to a small minority that would never again be able to be a political factor in Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of all this activity that was taking place before your very eyes, tell me, were there other public figures in Croatia who issued such threats to Serbs and repeated such threats from 1990s, early 1990s, that spoke of the intentions of the Croatian leadership?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some people in Croatia who also reacted against them. There was a very famous painter who said that Tudjman was trying to persuade him in the 1990s that he would resolve the Serb problem in Croatia by making half of the Serbs pack up and leave and would expel the rest. This was Edo Murtic, a very famous painter. And this theory originates from Mile Budak, whom I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we find that passage on page 95 in the next tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand this witness is going to be six hours, so we have to check what's actually happening at the moment. I can see that he's heavily dependent on his notes. His eyes are down on them throughout most questions. They seem to be very well ordered, with titled and subparagraphs, and probably constitute effectively a witness statement. I'm not sure how desirable it is to have a witness really following notes that closely unless they're available to everyone. If they are available to everyone, of course, we'll be able to read them between now and whenever next week's sitting starts, maybe make some concessions or identify some areas of evidence that are not helpful. What we're now doing is going through books -- for example, the last one, last entry on tab 7, I'm not sure whether the witness says he was present at the event itself. If he was, he can give evidence of it, if it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's noticeable that we've got no direct evidence yet. You would think a man in the parliament who was actually encountering Mr. Tudjman would be able to tell us something directly about what he was saying and doing, to the extent that it's relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I respectfully adopt Your Honour's observations. The material is by and large not translated, we've only had it since last Wednesday afternoon, and the answers, as I say some of them are very well cast and formulated, appear to be quite well prepared. So I think -- I would respectfully invite the Chamber to first of all question the admissibility of books, and we had some quite interesting passages in the cross-examination of my learned friend of the last witness where plainly relevant books were at best being admitted for identification only because the witness has no direct experience or declines or fails to acknowledge the accuracy of the book. Those don't go in as evidence. I'm not sure what the evidence or status of this material is. And there it is. I mean, it may be the better course would be to get the witness to turn his notes over, or perhaps he'd like to provide them to us and we'll copy them and peruse them over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Atlagic, what kind of notes do you have, and to what extent are you relying on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not relying on these notes. They are just bullet points, and I can do without them if I have to. I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, to your question, the witness already answered that he made some bullet points for himself over the past three days. I think he is entitled to them. If you think that he shouldn't be looking at notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explained that first. But, Mr. Milosevic, as to the nature of this witness's evidence, are you going to lead him to evidence that is more directly related to the charges in the indictments, and is there any evidence coming from him of matters in which he was more directly involved?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Nice mentioned tab 7, for instance. I'm going to take this as an example because he mentioned it. A quotation was used from Tudjman's speech before the parliament, his state of the nation speech, saying that the Serbs were reduced to an insignificant minority and would never again be a political factor. That's a public document. It's his speech before the Croatian parliament. Can anybody dispute that it's a valid document if we are looking at a speech of a president, a head of state, before the parliament of that state? And the witness is a man who was a politician at the time in Croatia, at the critical time in the early 1990s, and he was politically active in that particular political scene. And even when he quotes, he quotes from what is already in the tabs. There is not a single quotation that he used that is not supported by the documents under the tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah. The witness may refer to the bullet points which he has -- which he has made, but of course to the extent that you don't have to refer to them, then so much the better because we prefer evidence to be given unaided. And, Mr. Milosevic, you must bring this witness to events in which he was more directly involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. I would be working in that direction as well. But this man was active in the political life, and all these are facts from political life. They are public. It's not about his secret conversations with Tudjman. These are public statements that marked the entire political atmosphere that prevailed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We haven't heard one word so far about anything he himself did or, indeed, experienced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come to that as well. Can I continue, please, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you have just said about the painter Edo Murtic, can we see it in tab 8, page 95, the penultimate paragraph? Can you please read that.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: "In his interview to Novi List, a newspaper from Rijeka, given in January 2000, Croatian painter Edo Murtic emphasises that Tudjman was assuring him on the eve of their 1990 elections that his objective was to achieve what the Ustashas and Pavelic had failed to do in 1941. He said 250.000 Serbs would pack up and leave and the remaining 250.000 would either remain or disappear."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look now at tab 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this more of the same, Mr. Milosevic, to show the state of mind of Tudjman? Haven't we had enough material on that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concerns Bosniaks. Tab 5 relates to Bosniaks -- sorry, tab 9 relates to Bosniaks, not Serbs, and I think it would be useful for the witness to deal with it. It's at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll try to deal with it very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He thought -- what did he believe?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: At the 4th Congress of the Croatian Democratic Union, Tudjman said, I quote: "A nation name of Bosniaks will make it easier for Muslims to make that mental choice in Croatia, because if there are Bosniaks in Bosnia of Muslim faith, it is clear that in Croatia there will be no Bosniaks of Croatian faith. They can only be Croats of Muslim faith."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us from your experience at that time, what did the HDZ focus its activities on when they came into power?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: When they came into power, the Croatian Democratic Union focused their activity on Croatisation, based mainly on the Ustasha fascist ideology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is a general assessment you're giving us. Could you give us a few examples of this Croatisation? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Names with any anti-fascist emblems were renamed with fascist iconography introduced. Everything, every name or symbol that had to do with the anti-fascist struggle from 1941 to 1945 is eliminated. And then there was a series of laws enacted from the 1990s onwards. For instance, laws were named for forests in Croatia. From 1990s onwards, when the HDZ was in power, every name of a law was -- began with the word "Croat"; "Croat forests," "Croat economy," et cetera. Also, a ban was introduced on placing flowers on the monument in the former concentration camp of Jasenovac for the victims there. The cleansing of Serbs from government authorities began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: As soon as Tudjman came into power. In June or maybe end May 1990, this purge of the Serbs began, not only from the police force but also from the Territorial Defence, ministries, et cetera. It was general Croatisation that was under way. Even in schools Serbs were no longer allowed to teach the Serbo-Croat language, because in the meantime the Croat language had been introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything physical happen regarding attitude to homes, Serbs' children, Serb lands, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Even names were changed of Serbs, Serb children, even elderly people. Then there was the attitude to homes and things that were sacred. In mid-1990s, there were attacks on things that Serbs held sacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the bombing of houses start?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1990 or the 1990s? Because the 1990s is a whole decade.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I'm talking only about 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us be clear, because the transcript refers to 1990s. I'm talking about the 1990, when the HDZ came into power, and even before that, things that Serbs held sacred were under attack. In Ilok 60 Serb tombstones were destroyed. The crosses were removed from them. Even fresh graves were destroyed. There was also an attack, a provocation, against a Serb Orthodox Church in Split. Graffiti, like "Serb sons of bitches," et cetera. The 3rd July in Dalmatia, a Serb was attacked by a Croat. One Miroslav Mlinar was stabbed to death in Benkovac [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1990. When?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Benkovac is your municipality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's where I was born, and that was my constituency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally familiar with the event? Did you see this Mlinar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a student of mine when he was in high school. And when that happened, I visited him at the hospital. I was an MP at the time. I saw that he had been stabbed three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did the authorities do about this?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Mainly nothing. Some sort of proceedings were started but came to nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said Serb houses were bombed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, could I ask, what did you do about it then when you saw that nothing was being done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was an MP for the Alliance of Socialists for the constituency of Benkovac, but other MPs, Croats, did not want to cooperate with me because I was of Serb ethnicity. And even in the Croatian parliament, a colleague of mine was attacking me with all sorts of insinuations and slander. That was the attitude to me. As soon as the HDZ came into power, they made it clear they would not be negotiating with Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was this is a young man, you say, stabbed to death in your constituency, where the majority of people must have supported you. What did you do about it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, he was stabbed but he wasn't stabbed to death. He was still alive afterwards. I did what I could. I tried in the Croatian Assembly to raise a question to the house, to the president of the Assembly and the president of the Executive Council of Croatia. That's what I did. I asked a question in the house. And that was my duty as an MP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier said that this person was stabbed to death. Is that wrong? You gave the name Miroslav Mlinar was stabbed to death in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was not stabbed to death. He -- he remained alive. It was an interpreter's error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see. And then it takes several questions before you tell us what you actually did about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Atlagic, you said that the Serbs at the beginning even started changing their names.

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, some did change their names out of fear. They changed their first and last names. And there were physical assaults as well on both the Serbs and on things they held sacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you give us examples? Can you quote examples of violence against the Serbs in addition to the ones you've already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can. I can give you the example or, rather, many examples in Sibenik, for example. Bore Petrovic, a case in point. His child was kidnapped. The child was taken away some ten kilometres from Sibenik, and a metal rod was used to beat and stab it. You could see traces on the body of this violence. On and the 21st of November, as well, 1990, a policeman in Benkovac was killed. Goran Alavanja was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was in 1990, was it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances of the killing of this policeman?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, I can't remember whether it was a day before a day after, I went to attend an Assembly meeting. I was in Zagreb, and I had my suspicions, because from Benkovac to Zagreb I saw a lot of policemen I didn't know, both in my municipality and the neighbouring municipality, and straight after that we received information that this event had taken place with Goran Alavanja, the policeman in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that tells me nothing about -- that tells me nothing about it. Was he a Serb? And in any event, what's the relevance of one -- this isolated incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not an isolated incident. It was an attempt at a killing in the 1990 -- or, rather, in 1990. Now we have a dead policeman. So can you imagine the disquiet among the Serb population, and the Croat population as well for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's with great sadness that all this material wasn't served in advance. It may be non-controversial and if it had been provided to us in advance we could have considered it and saved time maybe, but it's up to the accused how he spends his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Not to enumerate further, from what you've just told us, can we speak about that as being isolated cases or was it a series of events and incidents which indicated violence against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a leading question. Ask another question. Move to another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you've been telling us about, about this violence, is that characteristic only of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't characteristic only of 1990 but 1991 as well. So already in 1991 -- well, later on we had a series of attacks similar to these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you mention 1991, is that the time of certain events in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Events throughout Croatia were taking place, in Western Slavonia especially. That's the area where we had a situation where Serb houses were already being attacked and buildings they hold sacred. At the end of 1990 and 1991, many church buildings, religious buildings were destroyed and damaged. Destroyed and damaged. Up until March 1992, over 4.000 houses were set fire to in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So 4.000 houses were set aflame?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, until March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What happened in Zadar, for example, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the Zadar affair, as it was known, the Crystal Night, when in Zadar, in 1991, 350 houses were blown up, and cafes, belonging to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us, was there any tension caused by the Serbs in Zadar at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: No, no tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen in Zadar in 1991? When was that event?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was either March or May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But anyway, the first half of 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this topic I think if we're going to be helped at all, do we not need to know whether he's speaking from his own firsthand experience that he was in Zadar or if he's perhaps, I don't know, quoting from a newspaper report or gossip or something? It might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the source of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of my information? Well, I was a national deputy, and the Zadar municipality is a neighbouring municipality just 15 kilometres away, and there was still communication between the people of the two municipalities. So I was in Zadar during those days to see what was going on, but it was a very well-known event that this -- what was referred to as the Crystal Night event took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about the events that happened at the foot of Mount Papuk and Psunj, the Serb villages there and what happened there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, around Psunj and Papuk, there were about 100 -- or over 100 Serb villages that were destroyed. They were destroyed, set fire to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we're talking about the end of 1991, are we?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you hear of the expression "The Serbs are flowing down the river towards Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of that. It was dominant in Western Slavonia, Baranja and Srem when corpses, which were massacred -- or, rather, Serb corpses which were massacred were thrown in the river and they flowed down the river toward Serbia. But I have to say that that was nothing new, because that was what happened in 1941 to 1945. You would see the same slogans written up. For instance, "King Peter, go to Belgrade," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We really have got to try, if I may respectfully suggest, to get some order into this witness's evidence. The accused asked him, it might be thought to be a slightly leading question, whether he had heard a particular expression. He had heard it and then he gave -- went on to give what appears to be, perhaps possibly a prepared, almost, or considered answer, but doesn't actually say where he heard it, who said it, what it amounts to. How are we being helped by this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: These are matters that you can raise in cross-examination, Mr. Nice. But, Mr. Milosevic, you really need to bring this witness to evidence of matters that he can speak of more directly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think he is directly speaking about this, too, and a moment ago, at Mr. Nice's direct intervention, he said that Zadar was the neighbouring municipality to his and that he personally travelled to Zadar and saw it all personally and that he personally communicated with the citizens and inhabitants who were part of his constituency and that he knows it all from firsthand information, not from the press and the mass media, because he was a national deputy, and some of his preoccupations involved what was going on, of course. May I be allowed to continue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but we would like -- we would like evidence that is more directly related to the matters in the indictment. We have had enough of this background.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All those atrocities are directly related because they lead to reaction, refugees, self-organisation, displaced persons, and things like that; self-defence. Directly connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But let's not speak about 1941 and 1945, Mr. Atlagic. Tell us what happened in 1990, in those years. You talked about Slavonia, and you spoke about the expression "The Serbs flowing down towards Serbia." What happened in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in the 1990s the situation was the similar in Slavonia. Sacred Serb buildings were attacked. In Vinkovci in 1990, for example, the library, Branka Egic Library, was set fire to. And I remember that particular event. So it's not only 1991 that is important. It all started in 1990 and went on to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about the facts and figures related to burnt-down Serb houses and Serbs killed during that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that at that time up until 1992 there were many Orthodox buildings throughout Croatia which were destroyed, either totally destroyed or partially destroyed, and I can even take the parishes one by one: The Dalmatian parish, the Karlovac parish, and all the six parishes that exist. So I can take it parish-by-parish. But up until 1990 and 1992, there were over 170 Serb sacred buildings that were either totally destroyed or damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "sacred buildings," do you mean churches, monasteries, or what?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Mostly churches and monasteries, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how many were destroyed until March 1992, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Over 160. Over 160 churches and monasteries were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Atlagic, did this sort of behaviour cause the Serbs to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This behaviour at the time - and it's 1990 - we can't speak of Serb crimes. In 1990 in my constituency, for example, I don't know of a single --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the destruction of buildings up until March 1992, and I'd like to know if -- Mr. Milosevic keeps telling us the point of this is that the Serbs reacted. Now, did Serbs commit crimes because of this sort of conduct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they didn't commit crimes only because of this kind of conduct but because crimes were committed against the Serbs. For example, over 200 Serbs in Western Slavonia, up until 1991 and March 1992 were -- died or were killed or destroyed and as many territorials were wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you at the end of the day going to be telling us that you don't know of any crimes that Serbs committed or are you going to be telling us about crimes which Serbs did commit and try to explain why they were committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were crimes committed on all sides, and that is not contentious. It is not contentious that there were individual crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will at some stage come to deal with the crimes that are alleged in the indictment perhaps. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please - and you're talking about 1990 and 1991 now - whether the Serbs, to the best of your knowledge, caused a situation for which the authorities had reason to retaliate. You're talking about villages burnt down, houses destroyed, churches and monasteries destroyed and damaged. Did the Serbs do anything which would trigger off retaliation of the kind you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: During that time, Serbs didn't react at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said 1990. You weren't referring to the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: MARKO ATLAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1990 the Serbs didn't give cause for -- well, it was all Serb -- I don't know any situation which was caused -- any untoward situation that was caused by the Serbs in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me take an example.
